subtopic_detail: Segmental facial infantile haemangioma with persistent stridor indicating subglottic airway involvement
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 month old girl whose parents report two weeks of a harsh cough and noisy breathing. She was treated for croup by her general practitioner four days ago with a single dose of oral dexamethasone, with no improvement.

She has a flat red patch covering her chin, lower lip and the front of her neck that was first noticed at 3 weeks of age and has been enlarging since. She has remained afebrile throughout and is feeding more slowly than usual.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 80/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor audible at rest with intercostal and suprasternal recession, confluent bright red plaque over the chin, lower lip and anterior neck, chest clear on auscultation, no drooling and no toxic appearance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe
options.rationale: Croup causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor over a few days in a child usually older than 6 months, with a febrile viral prodrome, and it responds to a single dose of corticosteroid. Two weeks of progressive afebrile stridor that did not respond to dexamethasone is not croup, and repeating the dose tests a diagnosis already excluded by the course. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Refer urgently for flexible laryngoscopy of the upper airway
options.rationale: A segmental haemangioma in the beard distribution carries roughly a 60 per cent risk of a synchronous subglottic haemangioma, which proliferates over the same months and presents as biphasic stridor unresponsive to steroid. Direct visualisation confirms the airway lesion, grades the degree of narrowing and allows propranolol to be started with appropriate monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Commence oral propranolol at home with weekly phone review
options.rationale: Propranolol is the correct drug for a subglottic haemangioma and often shrinks it within days, but starting it at home in an infant with stridor at rest and recession leaves an unsecured airway and unmonitored risks of hypoglycaemia, bradycardia and hypotension. The near miss to hold onto is that the drug is right and the setting is wrong: initiation belongs in hospital once the airway has been assessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and treat for bacterial tracheitis
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, a toxic appearance and rapid deterioration over hours, whereas this infant has been afebrile and well perfused for two weeks. A chest radiograph cannot assess the subglottis adequately and would delay definitive visualisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Arrange ultrasound of the neck lesion and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Ultrasound characterises the cutaneous lesion and can confirm a high flow vascular anomaly, but it cannot visualise the subglottis and therefore does not answer the question the stridor is asking. Two weeks of observation spans the period of most rapid haemangioma proliferation. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate until around 5 months and then involute slowly over years, so most need no treatment. The exceptions are lesions that threaten function or life, and a segmental haemangioma over the chin, lower lip and anterior neck is the classic marker for airway involvement because the subglottic lesion follows the same developmental segment. Such infants are typically misdiagnosed as having recurrent croup, and the clue is that the stridor is biphasic, progressive over weeks, afebrile and unresponsive to corticosteroid. Propranolol has replaced systemic corticosteroid and tracheostomy as first line treatment and usually produces rapid improvement, but initiation requires baseline assessment for cardiac and glycaemic risk.
key_points: Beard distribution segmental haemangioma predicts subglottic involvement in a majority of infants
Biphasic progressive stridor in an afebrile infant under 6 months is not croup
Flexible laryngoscopy is the assessment that confirms and grades the airway lesion
Propranolol is first line treatment but is initiated with monitoring, not by telephone
Large segmental facial haemangiomas also warrant assessment for associated cerebrovascular and cardiac anomalies
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for infantile haemangioma is started at a low dose and uptitrated towards 2 to 3 mg/kg/day in divided doses, with feeding maintained every 4 to 6 hours because the main serious adverse effect in infants is hypoglycaemia during fasting or intercurrent illness.

subtopic_detail: Right sided varicocele that fails to decompress when supine as a marker of retroperitoneal pathology
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 13 year old boy who noticed a dull ache in his right scrotum after football and told his mother it feels like a bag of worms above his right testicle. The ache has been present for about six weeks and is worse at the end of the day.

He has had no fever, no urinary symptoms and no weight loss. He is in Tanner stage 3 and his height is tracking along the 50th centile.

data_table.Scrotal examination: Soft non-tender mass of distended veins above the right testis that persists unchanged when he lies flat, left hemiscrotum normal, both testes 12 mL and equal in size and consistency
data_table.Abdominal examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass or organomegaly, no inguinal hernia, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and review in 12 months with testicular volume measured
options.rationale: Annual review with volume measurement is reasonable surveillance for a typical left sided adolescent varicocele that decompresses when supine and is not causing testicular growth arrest. Applying that plan to a right sided varicocele that does not decompress accepts a year of delay for a possible retroperitoneal mass. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer for varicocele embolisation by interventional radiology
options.rationale: Embolisation treats the varicocele itself and is considered for pain, testicular growth arrest or abnormal semen parameters, but treating the dilated veins without establishing why they are obstructed leaves the cause untreated. Intervention should follow, not precede, the search for an obstructing lesion. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.text: Arrange a scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and review the result
options.rationale: Scrotal ultrasound confirms venous dilatation and measures testicular volumes, both of which are already evident clinically, and it does not image the retroperitoneum where the answer lies. The near pair to separate is that scrotal imaging characterises the varicocele while abdominal imaging explains it. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer to urology for elective varicocelectomy within 6 months
options.rationale: Surgical ligation is an option for symptomatic varicocele with growth arrest, and the indication has not been established here since the testes are equal in volume. It also carries the same flaw as embolisation, namely treating the venous consequence while the retroperitoneal cause goes unexamined. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

options.text: Arrange abdominal imaging to exclude a retroperitoneal mass
options.rationale: Around 90 per cent of adolescent varicoceles are left sided because the left gonadal vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, so an isolated right sided varicocele is anatomically unexpected. Failure to decompress on lying flat indicates fixed obstruction to venous drainage rather than reflux, and both features together mandate imaging of the retroperitoneum for a renal or retroperitoneal mass. (Source: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Varicocele affects roughly 15 per cent of adolescent boys and is almost always left sided, a consequence of the left gonadal vein entering the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer column of blood above the valves. The two findings that break that pattern are a right sided varicocele and a varicocele that does not empty when the patient lies down, and either should prompt imaging of the retroperitoneum for a mass obstructing venous return. Routine management of an ordinary left varicocele is observation with annual testicular volume measurement, since most cause no harm and intervention is reserved for pain, a volume differential above 20 per cent or abnormal semen analysis in older adolescents. The clinical examination that matters is therefore done both standing and supine.
key_points: About 90 per cent of varicoceles are left sided for anatomical reasons
An isolated right sided varicocele is an indication for retroperitoneal imaging
Failure to decompress when supine indicates fixed obstruction rather than valvular reflux
Routine left varicoceles are observed with annual testicular volume measurement
Intervention is indicated for pain, a volume differential above 20 per cent or abnormal semen parameters
explanation.pearls: Examine every varicocele both standing and lying flat; a varicocele that persists when supine has a fixed obstructive cause and needs retroperitoneal imaging, whatever side it is on.

sources.label: RACGP: Scrotal lumps in children and adolescents
RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic neonate with pulmonary venous congestion and a normal cardiac silhouette in whom prostaglandin is harmful
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital 400 kilometres from the nearest paediatric cardiac surgical centre, where there is no echocardiography available overnight. A term male infant born 6 hours ago by normal vaginal delivery has developed worsening respiratory distress and cyanosis.

He was given 100 per cent oxygen by headbox 20 minutes ago with no change in his saturations. The consultant is driving in. Your resident has drawn up prostaglandin E1 and is asking you to confirm the infusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 80 breaths per minute, SpO2 78 percent right hand and 77 percent right foot, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession with grunting, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, no murmur audible, femoral pulses present and equal to brachial pulses
data_table.Chest radiograph: Normal cardiac silhouette with cardiothoracic ratio 0.52, diffuse ground glass opacification of both lung fields with septal lines, no pneumothorax
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.18, PaCO2 38 mmHg, PaO2 32 mmHg on 100 percent oxygen, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate and ventilate and arrange urgent cardiac surgical transfer
options.rationale: Severe cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, with pulmonary venous congestion on a normal sized heart and equal pre and post ductal saturations, indicates obstructed pulmonary venous return, in which the obstruction lies downstream of the lungs and no amount of ductal patency helps. Intubation with positive pressure recruits the oedematous lung and buys time, while the only definitive treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction at a cardiac centre. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanogram per kilogram per minute
options.rationale: Prostaglandin is the correct reflex for most duct dependent cyanotic lesions, but the picture here is pulmonary venous obstruction, where increasing pulmonary blood flow through a patent duct raises pulmonary venous return against a fixed obstruction and worsens the pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia. The findings that break the default are a normal cardiac silhouette with pulmonary oedema and equal pre and post ductal saturations with present femoral pulses. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

options.text: Give a 20 mL per kilogram sodium chloride 0.9 percent fluid bolus
options.rationale: Volume expansion is the reflex for shock with poor perfusion, but this infant has an enlarged liver and interstitial pulmonary oedema, indicating a congested rather than an underfilled circulation. Further volume worsens pulmonary venous pressure and the oedema that is already causing the hypoxaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

options.text: Commence nasal CPAP with intravenous frusemide and fluid restriction
options.rationale: This is the treatment of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure, and diuresis cannot relieve a fixed anatomical obstruction to pulmonary venous drainage. Nasal CPAP is also inadequate respiratory support for an infant with a pH of 7.18 who needs transfer by air or road. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography before starting any other treatment
options.rationale: Echocardiography is the definitive diagnostic test and will be performed, but it is unavailable on this site overnight and waiting for it leaves a profoundly acidotic infant unsupported. Stabilisation and activation of the retrieval service happen first and in parallel with, not after, diagnostic imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: The cyanosed neonate)

explanation.summary: Cyanosis in a newborn that does not improve with high inspired oxygen points to a structural cardiac cause or to persistent pulmonary hypertension, and prostaglandin E1 is the standard holding treatment because most such lesions depend on the duct for either pulmonary or systemic flow. Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage is the important exception: the pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation through a channel that is narrowed, so the lungs are congested while the heart is small, and opening the duct increases flow into an already obstructed system. The radiographic signature is a normal or small cardiac silhouette with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion, which is routinely misread as respiratory distress syndrome or congenital pneumonia. It is one of the few congenital cardiac lesions that is a true surgical emergency, because no catheter or drug intervention relieves the obstruction.
key_points: Cyanosis unresponsive to 100 per cent oxygen indicates a cardiac or pulmonary vascular cause
Pulmonary venous congestion with a normal sized heart is the signature of obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
Prostaglandin worsens obstructed pulmonary venous return rather than helping it
Equal pre and post ductal saturations with present femoral pulses argue against duct dependent systemic obstruction
Definitive treatment is immediate surgical repair, so retrieval is activated at the same time as stabilisation
explanation.pearls: In a cyanosed neonate, read the chest radiograph before committing to prostaglandin: pulmonary oedema on a normal sized heart means obstructed pulmonary venous drainage, where prostaglandin worsens hypoxaemia and only surgery helps.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism and short stature requiring karyotype
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old girl who has never had a period. Her mother is 168 cm tall and had menarche at 12 years.

She is doing well at school, exercises twice a week, eats a varied diet and her weight has been stable. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and reports a normal sense of smell.

data_table.Examination: Height 148 cm which is below the 1st centile, body mass index 22 kg/m2, Tanner stage 1 breast development, Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, normal external genitalia, no clitoromegaly, blood pressure equal in both arms
data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L (follicular 3 to 9), LH 24 IU/L (follicular 2 to 10), oestradiol 42 pmol/L (follicular 110 to 400), prolactin 310 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside low oestradiol, which is hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, or when prolactin is elevated. Here the gonadotrophins are markedly raised, which localises the problem to the ovary rather than to the pituitary. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess uterine and ovarian morphology
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound is the right first test when primary amenorrhoea occurs with normal breast development, because it distinguishes outflow tract obstruction and Mullerian agenesis from other causes. With absent breast development and an FSH of 68 IU/L the ovary has already been identified as the site of the problem, and imaging would not explain why. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Karyotype analysis performed on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: Primary amenorrhoea with absent breast development, raised gonadotrophins and short stature is hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, and Turner syndrome is the commonest cause in this setting, so karyotype is the test that makes the diagnosis. It also identifies Y chromosome material, which mandates gonadectomy because of gonadoblastoma risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Repeat the gonadotrophins and oestradiol in three months
options.rationale: Repeat testing is appropriate when a single result is borderline or discordant with the clinical picture, whereas an FSH of 68 IU/L with absent breast development at 16 years is unambiguous and concordant. Deferring the diagnosis delays oestrogen replacement at the age when peak bone mass is accrued. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Measure serum anti Mullerian hormone and antral follicle count
options.rationale: Anti Mullerian hormone quantifies remaining ovarian reserve and will simply confirm that it is very low, which the FSH has already established. It provides no information about the underlying cause and does not alter the management that follows. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by asking two questions in sequence: is there breast development, which indicates oestrogen exposure, and is the uterus present. Absent breast development with raised gonadotrophins means the ovaries have failed, and in an adolescent the leading causes are Turner syndrome and its mosaic variants, gonadal dysgenesis and previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Short stature substantially raises the likelihood of Turner syndrome, which affects about 1 in 2500 live female births and is frequently not diagnosed until adolescence when puberty fails to progress. Diagnosis triggers a package of care that extends well beyond menstruation: cardiac imaging for bicuspid aortic valve and aortic coarctation, renal ultrasound, thyroid and coeliac screening, hearing assessment, and oestrogen replacement to induce puberty and protect bone.
key_points: Absent breast development with raised FSH localises the problem to the ovary
Turner syndrome is the commonest cause of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism with short stature
Karyotype rather than imaging is the diagnostic test in this pattern
Y chromosome material on karyotype mandates gonadectomy for gonadoblastoma risk
Diagnosis triggers cardiac, renal, thyroid, coeliac and hearing assessment
explanation.pearls: Every newly diagnosed girl with Turner syndrome needs echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, because bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation are present in up to 30 per cent and aortic dissection risk persists into pregnancy and adult life.

subtopic_detail: Discrete mobile breast lump in a woman under 35 requiring ultrasound led triple assessment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who found a lump in her right breast in the shower 6 weeks ago. It has not changed in size since, and she does not think it varies with her cycle.

She has no nipple discharge, no skin change and no breast pain. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill, has never been pregnant, and no one in her family has had breast or ovarian cancer.

data_table.Examination: Discrete 22 mm smooth firm mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, no skin dimpling, tethering or peau d'orange, nipple normal with no discharge on expression, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, left breast normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her and review the lump after her next menstrual period
options.rationale: Short interval review is reasonable for a vague area of nodularity that fluctuates with the cycle, whereas a discrete persistent lump requires imaging regardless of age. Although most lumps in this age group are benign, breast cancer does occur in young women and clinical examination alone cannot exclude it. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Arrange bilateral mammography and review her with the report
options.rationale: Mammography performs poorly in women under 35 because dense glandular tissue reduces sensitivity, and it delivers radiation to a young breast for limited diagnostic return. It is added to ultrasound when imaging or clinical findings are suspicious, rather than being the first line test at this age. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Refer her directly for surgical excision of the lump with histology
options.rationale: Excision is a treatment decision that follows characterisation, and many lesions of this type in this age group need no operation at all once imaging and needle biopsy confirm the diagnosis. Proceeding to surgery first exposes her to an unnecessary scar and anaesthetic. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Arrange breast ultrasound with core biopsy if imaging is not benign
options.rationale: Any discrete breast lump is assessed by triple assessment, combining clinical examination, imaging and needle biopsy, and ultrasound is the imaging of choice under 35 because it distinguishes cyst from solid lesion in dense young breast tissue. Core biopsy is added when the imaging is indeterminate or suspicious, or when the clinical and imaging findings disagree, which is the safeguard that makes the pathway safe in a young woman. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Stop the oral contraceptive pill and reassess the lump in 3 months
options.rationale: Hormonal contraception does not cause discrete breast lumps and stopping it will not resolve one, while three months of observation delays diagnosis. It also removes her contraception without addressing the presenting problem. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Every discrete breast lump is investigated by triple assessment, meaning clinical assessment, imaging and tissue sampling, and the diagnosis is only accepted when all three components agree. Age determines the imaging: ultrasound alone is the appropriate first test under 35 because young breast tissue is dense and mammographic sensitivity falls, while women over 35 have mammography and ultrasound together. A smooth, firm, mobile, well defined lump in a woman in her twenties is most often a fibroadenoma, which requires no treatment once confirmed unless it is large, growing or troublesome to the patient. Discordance between components is the safety net: a benign looking lesion with a clinically suspicious examination still requires biopsy. Features that raise concern at any age are a hard irregular fixed lump, skin dimpling or tethering, nipple retraction or bloody discharge, and palpable axillary nodes.
key_points: Triple assessment is clinical examination, imaging and needle biopsy, and all three must agree
Ultrasound is the first line imaging under 35; mammography is added from 35 onwards
A confirmed fibroadenoma needs no excision unless large, growing or symptomatic
Discordant components mandate biopsy even when imaging looks benign
Hard, fixed or irregular lumps, skin tethering and bloody nipple discharge are red flags
explanation.pearls: A fibroadenoma that grows rapidly over weeks to months, particularly beyond 5 cm, should be excised rather than observed, because a phyllodes tumour is clinically and radiologically indistinguishable and needs wide local excision with clear margins.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom
RACGP: Breast lumps in general practice

subtopic_detail: Overactive bladder without stress incontinence managed with conservative therapy before pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58 year old woman who describes a sudden overwhelming need to pass urine that she sometimes cannot defer, with leakage on the way to the toilet about three times a week. She voids around 11 times a day and wakes twice at night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She drinks four cups of coffee and two cups of tea daily. She had two normal vaginal births and went through menopause at 51 years.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no pelvic organ prolapse beyond the hymen on Valsalva, no leakage demonstrated on cough stress test, vulval and vaginal mucosa well oestrogenised, voluntary pelvic floor contraction present and sustained for 6 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for blood, nitrites and leucocytes, midstream urine culture no growth, post void residual volume 35 mL on bladder scan, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oxybutynin 5 mg orally twice daily and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy is second line, offered when conservative measures have been tried, and oxybutynin is the poorest choice in this class because of dry mouth, constipation and central anticholinergic effects that accumulate towards cognitive harm in older women. Starting it now skips the interventions that work for a substantial proportion of women without drug burden. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women)

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before deciding on further treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is indicated when conservative and drug treatment have failed, when surgery is being planned, or when the symptom pattern is mixed or discordant with examination findings. This is an unambiguous storage symptom picture with a normal post void residual and no stress leakage, so the test would not change the first step. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women)

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for consideration of a midurethral sling
options.rationale: A midurethral sling treats stress urinary incontinence, which is leakage on effort or exertion, and this woman explicitly does not leak on coughing, sneezing or lifting. Continence surgery for urgency incontinence does not help and can worsen storage symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women)

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream three nights weekly and reassess
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen helps storage symptoms when there is genitourinary syndrome of menopause with atrophic changes, and this woman's mucosa is described as well oestrogenised. Offering it here treats a finding that is not present. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women)

options.text: Start bladder training with a fluid and caffeine reduction programme
options.rationale: Bladder training with scheduled deferment, combined with pelvic floor muscle training and reduction of caffeine, is first line for overactive bladder and produces meaningful improvement in a large proportion of women over 6 to 12 weeks. This woman's six caffeinated drinks a day are a modifiable driver of both urgency and nocturia, and she has a demonstrable voluntary pelvic floor contraction to build on. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women)

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome of urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency incontinence, diagnosed once infection, haematuria, significant residual volume and glycosuria have been excluded. A bladder diary over three days is the most useful single assessment because it quantifies functional bladder capacity, fluid and caffeine intake and the true frequency, which patients routinely misestimate. First line treatment is behavioural: bladder training with progressive deferment, pelvic floor muscle training, caffeine reduction and weight loss where relevant. Drug treatment follows if symptoms persist, and the modern preference is a beta 3 agonist or a more bladder selective antimuscarinic rather than oxybutynin, particularly in older women, because of the association between cumulative anticholinergic burden and dementia.
key_points: Exclude infection, haematuria, raised residual volume and diabetes before labelling overactive bladder
A three day bladder diary quantifies intake, frequency and functional capacity
Bladder training, pelvic floor training and caffeine reduction are first line
Stress incontinence leaks on exertion and is the indication for a sling, not urgency incontinence
Urodynamics is reserved for failed treatment, mixed symptoms or preoperative assessment
explanation.pearls: When drug treatment becomes necessary, mirabegron avoids the anticholinergic load of oxybutynin but requires blood pressure monitoring because it can raise blood pressure, and it should be avoided in severe uncontrolled hypertension.

sources.label: NICE: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women

subtopic_detail: Persistent offensive vaginal discharge in a young woman with negative sexually transmitted infection testing
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 19 year old woman with 5 weeks of vaginal discharge that she describes as brown and foul smelling, staining her underwear daily. It has not responded to a course of oral metronidazole or to an antifungal pessary.

A self-collected swab 3 weeks ago was negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas. She has no fever, no pelvic pain and no dyspareunia. Her periods are regular and she has never been pregnant.

data_table.Examination: Vulva normal, abdomen soft with no tenderness, no cervical motion tenderness and no adnexal mass on bimanual examination, uterus anteverted and normal size
data_table.Investigations: Repeat vaginal swab negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas, urine dipstick negative, beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a 7 day course of oral doxycycline and review after treatment
options.rationale: Doxycycline treats chlamydia and is part of pelvic inflammatory disease regimens, and both have been excluded by negative testing and the absence of cervical motion or adnexal tenderness. A third antimicrobial course repeats the pattern that has already failed twice. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge)

options.text: Perform a speculum examination and remove any object that is found
options.rationale: Persistent offensive or brown discharge that does not respond to antimicrobial treatment, in a woman with no systemic features and negative infection testing, is a retained vaginal foreign body until the vagina has been inspected, and a forgotten tampon is by far the commonest. Self-collected swabs do not involve inspection of the vaginal vault, which is why three courses of treatment can precede the diagnosis, and removal is immediately curative. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge)

options.text: Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound to assess the uterus and adnexae
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound assesses the uterus, endometrium and ovaries rather than the vaginal vault, and retained material is frequently not seen on it. A normal scan in this situation would falsely reassure while the cause remains in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge)

options.text: Take a high vaginal swab for culture and treat according to the result
options.rationale: Culture of a vaginal swab in this setting grows mixed anaerobic flora that reflect the underlying problem rather than identifying a treatable pathogen, so the result directs another antibiotic course at a secondary phenomenon. The swab is also typically taken at the same speculum examination that would reveal the cause directly. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge)

options.text: Perform a cervical screening test and await the laboratory report
options.rationale: Cervical screening in Australia begins at 25 years of age, so it is not indicated for a 19 year old, and it is a screening rather than a diagnostic test in a symptomatic woman. Cervical malignancy would in any case be assessed by examination and biopsy rather than by a screening result. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program)

explanation.summary: Vaginal discharge is usually physiological, bacterial vaginosis or candidiasis, with trichomonas, chlamydia and gonorrhoea the infections to exclude, but discharge that persists after appropriate treatment demands that the diagnosis be revisited rather than the treatment repeated. A retained foreign body, most often a tampon but sometimes a condom or a pessary, produces a characteristically offensive brown or blood stained discharge with a well woman and negative infection testing. The increasing use of self-collected swabs, while excellent for improving screening participation, means that a speculum examination may never happen unless it is deliberately arranged, and this is one of the diagnoses that falls through that gap. Removal resolves the symptoms within days and antibiotics are usually unnecessary. In older women the same picture requires exclusion of a fistula and of cervical or vaginal malignancy, and in prepubertal girls a foreign body is the leading cause of offensive or blood stained discharge.
key_points: Discharge that fails appropriate treatment should prompt review of the diagnosis, not another course
Offensive brown discharge with negative infection testing suggests a retained foreign body
Self-collected swabs do not include inspection of the vaginal vault
Ultrasound frequently does not show retained vaginal material
In older women the same presentation requires exclusion of fistula and malignancy
explanation.pearls: Australian cervical screening starts at 25 years and is repeated 5 yearly with primary human papillomavirus testing, so it has no role in assessing vaginal discharge in a symptomatic woman under that age.

subtopic_detail: Hirsutism with regular ovulatory cycles and mildly raised testosterone requiring 17 hydroxyprogesterone
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17 year old girl who has been waxing her upper lip and chin since she was 14 and now shaves her lower abdomen twice a week. She finds it distressing and wants to know why it is happening.

Her periods started at 12 years and come every 28 to 30 days lasting 5 days. Her voice has not changed, she has noticed no change in muscle bulk and no hair loss. Her father and paternal grandfather are of Lebanese background.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, terminal hair over the upper lip, chin, periareolar area and lower abdomen, no clitoromegaly, no temporal hair recession, no acanthosis nigricans, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.3 to 1.9), sex hormone binding globulin 48 nmol/L (26 to 110), DHEAS 6.1 micromol/L (1.0 to 9.0), prolactin 290 mIU/L (less than 500), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and measure ovarian volume
options.rationale: Ovarian morphology is not used to diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome within 8 years of menarche because multifollicular ovaries are a normal finding in adolescence, and this patient is 5 years post menarche. The scan would generate a finding that cannot be interpreted diagnostically at her age. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with morning cortisol
options.rationale: Screening for Cushing syndrome is warranted when there are specific features such as proximal myopathy, violaceous striae, easy bruising, central weight gain or hypertension, none of which are described. Testing without those features generates false positives in adolescents. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands and pelvis with contrast
options.rationale: Imaging for an androgen secreting tumour is triggered by rapid onset over months, frank virilisation with clitoromegaly and voice change, or testosterone above about 5 nmol/L, and this presentation has none of those. Irradiating an adolescent for a gradual 3 year history is not justified. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Early morning follicular phase 17 hydroxyprogesterone measurement
options.rationale: Non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia mimics polycystic ovary syndrome with hirsutism and mildly raised androgens, and it is specifically more prevalent in people of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern ancestry, so it must be excluded before the common diagnosis is accepted. The screening test is 17 hydroxyprogesterone taken in the early morning follicular phase, because the value falls later in the day and rises after ovulation. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Repeat total testosterone with free androgen index in three months
options.rationale: Repeating androgen measurement is useful when a single result is borderline or the sample timing was uncertain, whereas a clearly raised testosterone with normal sex hormone binding globulin is already informative. Repeating it does not distinguish between the two diagnoses that remain in play. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

explanation.summary: Hirsutism means terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution and is graded with the modified Ferriman Gallwey score, with the threshold varying by ethnicity. The great majority of cases are polycystic ovary syndrome or idiopathic, but non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency accounts for a meaningful minority and is far commoner in some populations, reaching several per cent in Ashkenazi Jewish, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern groups. It cannot be distinguished clinically from polycystic ovary syndrome, which is why 17 hydroxyprogesterone is measured rather than inferred. Regular ovulatory cycles make polycystic ovary syndrome less likely and raise the relative probability of the non classical enzyme deficiency or an idiopathic cause, while rapid onset with virilisation shifts the concern to an androgen secreting tumour.
key_points: Measure 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the early morning follicular phase, when the value is highest
Non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is clinically indistinguishable from polycystic ovary syndrome
Prevalence is substantially higher in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi Jewish populations
Ovarian ultrasound is not diagnostic within 8 years of menarche
Rapid virilisation or testosterone above about 5 nmol/L prompts imaging for a tumour
explanation.pearls: A follicular phase 17 hydroxyprogesterone below 6 nmol/L effectively excludes non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, while a higher value requires a short synacthen test to confirm it rather than treatment on the screening result alone.

sources.label: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

subtopic_detail: Secondary amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea and prolactin above 4000 requiring pituitary imaging
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 27 year old woman whose periods stopped 8 months ago after years of regular cycles. She has also noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers.

She has never been pregnant, uses condoms for contraception, takes no regular medication and no over the counter preparations. She has gained no weight, feels the cold no differently, and has had no headaches.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, no breast mass or lymphadenopathy, visual fields full to confrontation, no acne or hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 4820 mIU/L (less than 500), beta hCG negative, TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (9 to 25), FSH 3.1 IU/L (follicular 3 to 9), oestradiol 96 pmol/L (follicular 110 to 400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa
options.rationale: A prolactin above roughly 4000 mIU/L with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, once pregnancy, hypothyroidism and drug causes are excluded, indicates a prolactin secreting adenoma and requires imaging to determine whether it is a microadenoma or a macroadenoma. That distinction drives both the urgency of treatment and the need for formal visual field assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request a macroprolactin assay before proceeding to any imaging
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that produces a spuriously raised result in an asymptomatic woman, which is exactly why it is checked when the prolactin is modestly elevated without symptoms. This woman has amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a low oestradiol, so the hyperprolactinaemia is demonstrably biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly and repeat prolactin
options.rationale: Cabergoline is the treatment of choice for prolactinoma and will lower the prolactin whether the lesion is a microadenoma or a macroadenoma, which is the problem with starting it first. Treating before imaging removes the information needed to plan surveillance and to decide whether visual fields and neurosurgical input are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeds
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement does protect bone in a woman with a low oestradiol, but inducing withdrawal bleeds masks the amenorrhoea that is the main clinical marker of disease activity. It also leaves an unimaged pituitary lesion untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat the prolactin as a fasting cannulated sample in two weeks
options.rationale: A cannulated series avoids the modest stress related rise that can push a prolactin slightly above the reference range, and it is appropriate for values up to about twice the upper limit. A result nearly ten times the upper limit with concordant symptoms is not explained by venepuncture stress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hyperprolactinaemia causes secondary amenorrhoea by suppressing pulsatile gonadotrophin releasing hormone, producing a low or inappropriately normal FSH with a low oestradiol, and galactorrhoea occurs in about half of affected women. Pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism and drugs, particularly antipsychotics, metoclopramide and some antidepressants, are excluded before anything else because they are far commoner than tumours. The magnitude of elevation is informative: values below about 2000 mIU/L are often drug related, stress related or due to macroprolactin, while values above about 4000 mIU/L strongly suggest an adenoma and rise roughly with tumour size. A very large macroadenoma can paradoxically give a falsely low prolactin through assay saturation, known as the hook effect, which is why a large lesion with an unimpressive prolactin should prompt a diluted repeat sample.
key_points: Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism and drug causes before imaging
Prolactin above roughly 4000 mIU/L with symptoms indicates an adenoma
Magnetic resonance imaging distinguishes microadenoma from macroadenoma and guides follow up
Macroprolactin testing is for modest elevations without symptoms
Cabergoline is first line treatment but is started after imaging, not before
explanation.pearls: In a woman with a large pituitary mass and only a modestly raised prolactin, ask the laboratory for a serially diluted sample, because assay saturation by very high prolactin levels produces a falsely low result and misdirects treatment towards surgery.

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug selection in the first trimester for a woman already established on carbimazole
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 30 year old woman at 7 weeks in her first pregnancy. She was diagnosed with Graves disease 18 months ago and takes carbimazole 15 mg daily, which she has continued since her positive pregnancy test three weeks ago.

She reports no palpitations, tremor or heat intolerance and has gained no weight. She has not yet had a discussion about her medication in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Small smooth goitre, no bruit, no lid lag or proptosis, fine tremor absent, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: TSH 0.06 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 17 pmol/L (9 to 25), free T3 5.2 pmol/L (3.0 to 5.5), TSH receptor antibody 6.8 IU/L (less than 1.8), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her antithyroid medication?

options.text: Continue carbimazole 15 mg daily and recheck thyroid function monthly
options.rationale: Continuing carbimazole through organogenesis exposes the foetus to a recognised embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia and abdominal wall defects, with the critical window falling between about 6 and 10 weeks. Monthly biochemical monitoring manages her thyroid status but does nothing about that exposure. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication and monitor thyroid function 4 weekly
options.rationale: Stopping treatment altogether is an option only for women at low risk of relapse, typically those on a small dose with a normal TSH receptor antibody after prolonged remission. This woman has a suppressed TSH and a markedly positive receptor antibody, so withdrawal risks a thyrotoxic relapse with its associated miscarriage, preterm birth and pre-eclampsia risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch to propylthiouracil now and review thyroid function in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil carries a lower teratogenic risk than carbimazole and is the preferred agent through the first trimester, so the switch is made as early in pregnancy as possible and ideally before 10 weeks. Her positive receptor antibody and suppressed TSH mean treatment cannot simply be stopped, which is what makes substitution rather than withdrawal the right move. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily to her current carbimazole
options.rationale: Beta blockade controls adrenergic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis and she has none, so it treats a problem she does not have while leaving the teratogenic exposure in place. Prolonged beta blockade in pregnancy is also associated with foetal growth restriction and neonatal hypoglycaemia. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine ablation to be given after 12 weeks
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy at any gestation because it crosses the placenta and ablates the foetal thyroid, which begins concentrating iodine from around 10 to 12 weeks. It is a definitive option to discuss after delivery and after breastfeeding has ceased. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Graves disease in pregnancy requires balancing two harms: uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis, which increases miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia and thyroid storm, and antithyroid drug teratogenicity, which is greatest during organogenesis. Both thionamides carry risk, but the carbimazole and methimazole embryopathy pattern of aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia and abdominal wall defects is more severe than the milder facial and urinary tract anomalies reported with propylthiouracil, so propylthiouracil is preferred through the first trimester. Many units then switch back to carbimazole in the second trimester because propylthiouracil carries a small risk of severe hepatotoxicity with prolonged use. The dose is titrated to keep free T4 in the upper part of the non pregnant reference range using the lowest effective dose, because thionamides cross the placenta and can cause foetal hypothyroidism and goitre.
key_points: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester, carbimazole thereafter in most protocols
The critical teratogenic window is roughly 6 to 10 weeks, so switch as early as possible
A positive TSH receptor antibody predicts relapse and argues against stopping treatment
Titrate to free T4 in the upper part of the reference range using the lowest effective dose
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated throughout pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Measure TSH receptor antibody at 18 to 22 weeks in any woman with current or past Graves disease, including those treated by surgery or radioiodine, because a titre above three times the upper limit predicts foetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis and mandates serial growth and heart rate surveillance.
